title: Node chronograph and evacuation regulator for SLA-preserving maintenance
creator: Ethan Zhao
description:
Summary: Build 'Node Chronograph' (a time-and-state-aware maintenance scheduler) and an 'Evacuation Regulator' (a feedback controller for drain rates) to automate node lifecycle operations while preserving per-tenant throughput guarantees and SLOs. This ticket implements orchestration logic, safety guards, and a simulation harness for validating planned maintenance, hotpatches, and capacity-driven decommission flows.

Background: Current maintenance flows are largely static: fixed drain windows, fixed cordon orders, and conservative global backoffs. We still observe SLO spikes during large maintenance events because drain rates don't account for live throughput tails, KV cache prewarm costs, or tenant contract commitments. Existing work covers manual maintenance playbooks and some staged warmup logic, but we lack an automated regulator that closes the loop on live telemetry to adapt drain aggressiveness.

Goals:
- Create a scheduler (Node Chronograph) that expresses maintenance as epochs with flexibility for stagger, priority lanes, and tenant throughput contracts.
- Implement an Evacuation Regulator that adjusts per-node drain rate using feedback signals: live tail latency, token throughput, KV cache miss rate, and reserved throughput ledger.
- Provide a simulation harness (maintenance-sim) capable of running synthetic workloads and reproducing SLO-impact scenarios, including cold KV-warmup penalties and upstream reroute latency.
- Deliver safe rollout plan with feature gates, canary on low-traffic pools, automatic rollback thresholds, and operator overrides.

Non-Goals:
- This ticket does not implement new KV cache persistence mechanisms or deep kernel scheduling changes. Those are follow-ups.

Success Criteria:
- In simulation, maintenance events with the regulator exhibit <10% SLO violation delta vs baseline under identical workload.
- On canary fleet: no more than one customer SLO breach in first 72h, and automatic rollback triggers correctly on >2x predicted violation.
- Observe measurable reduction in peak tail latency during staged decommissions in production (target 15% improvement).

Design / Approach:
1) Node Chronograph: epoch model where each epoch has labeled maintenance intents (eg. security-patch, kernel-update, voluntary-decommission) and constraints (deadline, priority, tenant-guardrails). Chronograph emits planned node actions to an orchestration queue with time windows and soft/hard deadlines.
2) Evacuation Regulator: controller module that consumes chronograph intents and telemetry streams. Controller computes a per-node drain-rate parameter (requests/sec or percentage of traffic shifted per minute) using PID-ish control augmented by a lookahead model that factors KV cache rewarm cost. Controller respects tenant throughput contracts by reserving lanes and throttling non-reserved workloads.
3) Safety layer: preflight checks (service health, active tail latency, current reserved capacity), kill-switch predicates, and a staged prewarm step that iteratively warms top-K KV entries before full cordon.
4) Simulator: event-driven simulator that models tenants, request mixes, KV cache heatmaps, and host-level resource contention. Provide hooks to replay historical telemetry and run Monte Carlo maintenance scenarios.

Implementation plan (high level):
- Week 1 (spike): prototype chronograph affine model and regulator control law; implement simulator skeleton and a minimal orchestrator adapter.
- Week 2: extend simulator with KV-warmup cost model and tenant throughput contracts; integrate regulator PID with lookahead heuristics.
- Week 3: run large-scale sims against historical traces; tune thresholds and rollback heuristics; prepare canary config.
- Week 4: canary in non-critical region, collect telemetry, iterate.

Rollout & Mitigation: start with a single low-priority fleet slice. Use canary gating and progressive funneling into production regions with automated rollback on SLO delta > configured threshold. Operator dashboard exposes live regulator decisions and allows manual override per-epoch.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Control law complexity: simple PID is understandable but may underperform in non-linear KV warmup regimes; ML model would be more adaptive but increases ops burden. We will start with a PID+heuristics approach.
- Tenant reservation enforcement: do we opt for soft reservation (best-effort throttling) or hard reservation (capacity carved out)? Start with soft enforcement and instrument customer impact.
- Simulator fidelity: balancing performance of simulator vs realism; initial focus on fast Monte Carlo to tune thresholds.

Risks:
- Mis-calibrated drain aggressiveness causing cascading retries and KV trauma. Mitigation: conservative defaults, staged prewarm, and fast rollback.
- Insufficient telemetry resolution leading to poor feedback signals. Mitigation: temporarily increase sampling for canary fleets during rollout.

Metrics to track:
- per-fleet 99th and 95th latency delta during maintenance windows (time-series).
- regulator action log (drain-rate changes, prewarm attempts, overrides).
- number of automatic rollbacks and time-to-rollback.
- customer-facing error rates and reserved-throughput violations.
